_about: Blueprint of every Onsurity JD: which sections exist, in what order, what each one is for, which visual component holds it, and how much space it has. The only fixed words are the section labels and headings (structure) and the company content in company/company.json. Everything inside a section is written fresh for each role from the user's input and that run's research. Capacity limits keep the page layout intact; they are not style rules.

header.purpose: Who is hiring, which function, where, and the role title, followed by a short summary of the role and one factual sentence (printed in bold sans) naming the main outcome the role is accountable for.

slots.title: Role title as it will be advertised; a specialisation may follow a comma
slots.lead: Summary of the role at this level
slots.punchline: One plain, factual sentence naming the main outcome this role is accountable for. It is printed in bold sans at the end of the lead. It is a fact, not a slogan.

meta.purpose: Five facts at a glance. Values are short (1–4 words). TRACK is Individual contributor, People manager or Player-coach. EXPERIENCE is a range like '3–5 years' or '6+ years'. The fifth cell is whichever of the options is most useful for this role; three items at most, joined by ' · '.

the_role.label: THE ROLE
the_role.heading: What this job actually is
the_role.purpose: A one-sentence opening line (section-lead style), then paragraphs that explain what the person will be responsible for, what the work involves day to day, who they work with, and why the role matters to the business.

the_level.label: THE LEVEL
the_level.heading: What {level_name} means here
the_level.purpose: A short opening line, then six key/value rows that describe the seniority expected. Each key is one upper-case word naming a dimension of seniority chosen by the research for this role; each value says what is expected on that dimension at this level.

your_work.label: YOUR WORK
your_work.purpose: The responsibilities, grouped into 3–4 areas. Each group has a short upper-case label (1–2 words) chosen by the research for this role, followed by bullets. Each bullet is one concrete responsibility.

the_bar.label: THE BAR

fixed.heading: How we expect you to operate

the_bar.purpose: The highlighted box. A one-line intro, then five behaviours this role cannot succeed without, each a short title (2–6 words) and a description. Chosen by the research for this role.

ai.label: AI
ai.heading: How we expect you to use AI
ai.purpose: How AI tools are used in this specific role today: an opening line and bullets naming real tools and real tasks for this function, plus where human judgement must stay in charge.

minimum.label: MINIMUM
minimum.heading: Minimum qualifications
minimum.purpose: Must-have requirements in two columns. Optional one-line note above. Each item starts with a short bold phrase naming the requirement (written **like this**), then the detail of what counts as meeting it.

preferred.label: PREFERRED
preferred.heading: Preferred qualifications
preferred.purpose: Nice-to-have experience that makes a candidate stronger. One line each.

toolkit.heading: What you'd work with
toolkit.purpose: The tools of the job as key/value rows: a lower-case category, then a comma-separated list. Optional one-line note above.

assessment.label: THE BAR, TESTED
assessment.heading: What we'll assess
assessment.purpose: An opening line, then exactly six cards (a 3×2 grid). Each card is one thing the hiring process will assess for this role: a title of 1–4 words and a description of what is tested and how.

not_for_you.label: READ TWICE
not_for_you.heading: This role is probably not for you if
not_for_you.purpose: Honest reasons a candidate might not enjoy this role. Each item completes the heading's sentence.

limits._about: Space each block has on the page: [min, max] words per item and [min, max] items, plus total_words, the ceiling that keeps a JD to about 7 pages. These protect the layout. validate_jd.py enforces them.
